title: Greek City-States
capsule: The Greek city-states (poleis) were independent urban communities that constituted the dominant political form of the Aegean world from the archaic period (c. 800 BCE) through the Hellenistic era, each with its own laws, magistracies, coinage, and cult calendar. At their height in the classical fifth and fourth centuries the poleis included Athens — which under Pericles (d. 429 BCE) operated a direct democracy and an Aegean empire of some 150–300 tribute-paying subjects — and Sparta, whose oligarchic-militarist constitution dominated the Peloponnese. The Macedonian conquests of Philip II (359–336 BCE) and Alexander the Great reduced most poleis to subordinate status, though many retained internal autonomy within Hellenistic kingdoms. Roman conquest of Greece between 229 and 146 BCE progressively absorbed the poleis into the provincial system, and the sack of Corinth in 146 BCE conventionally marks the end of the political independence of the last significant polis leagues.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Greek city-states as a collective entity resist precise territorial bounding; the dataset polygon presumably aggregates the Greek world broadly, but individual polis territories are unevenly attested and the outer extent (Magna Graecia, Black Sea colonies) complicates any single-polygon representation.
